newsitem.title: SPAIN: Endesa rises, electric protocol seen neutral. [CORRECTED 12:13 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Endesa rises, electric protocol seen neutral. [CORRECTED 12:13 GMT]

text.p: Spanish electricity firm Endesa was strongly higher on Friday amid expectations that an upcoming framework for new sector regulations would be something of a non-event, dealers and analysts said.
At 1120 GMT, Endesa was up 90 pesetas, 1.06 percent, to 8,580, while the Ibex index was up 0.5 percent to 4,638.31.

"It seems they're going to leave the subject of sunk costs out of the protocol because it's too difficult to resolve quickly. This was something weighing on (the shares) because Endesa has the most quantity of sunk costs, so in a way its a victory for (the firm)," said a dealer at a Spanish bank.
The stock could rise to about 8,700 pesetas short-term, the dealer added.

Sunk costs were broadly defined by one analyst as those which under the present electricity regime are compensated to some degree by the government, which would fall away under the fully competitive framework which the government plans.
These would include coal generation costs, a political bone of contention.
Local press reports, speculating on the possibility of what may be contained in the electricity protocol, have been indicating that the thorny subject of sunk costs will be left off the agenda.
The industry ministry declined to comment.

But analysts believe that negotiations between the government and electricity firms have yet to reach an agreement on these costs. For this reason the protocol, due to be signed on December 5, will likely leave the subject aside.
An accord on this key issue could take a further six months to materialise, said one analyst, who requested anonymity.
"The protocol will be pretty lightweight," he said.

"I think it could take them another six months before they come up with something concrete, and even then its not going to be anything that really damages Endesa because (the government) has got its eye on the placement," he added.
In principle, the government is due to sell its remaining 67 percent remaining stake in Endesa on the stock market in the second half of 1997 (Corrects from 1996).

"My impression is that the way the (electricity regulations) are going to be changed will be both slow and limited," said a Standard & Poor's analyst. "Liberalisation has to be mild, and there is a strong motivation to avoid damages to Endesa."
On Thursday, S&P's reaffirmed its long term ratings on Endesa and took the utility off CreditWatch.
S&P's considered that after Endesa's bid for the remaining 75 percent of regional utilities Sevillana and Fecsa its financial health was still strong.
This was another factor underpinning flows into the stock, dealers said.

Furthermore, worries over the protocol have been holding the share price back in the past six months, dealers said. As time goes on the market seems more and more convinced that changes to the firm will have a limited impact.
